found.lens: Metrology/experimental-history lens: I read papers where the *number* carries as much convention as the equation does — calibration-scale realizations, epoch-dependent unit definitions, instrument-native units, and uncertainty statements. The tool's coverage is essentially complete on the *algebraic* side (which constants are set to 1, which 4π sits where). What it has almost nothing on is the *value* side: a quantity in an old paper is not (number, dimension) but (number, dimension, realization-of-the-unit, medium/reference state, uncertainty semantics). Every gap below is invisible to dimensional analysis by construction — both variants have identical dimensions, and the wrong one is usually within a factor of 1.5 of the right one, so no order-of-magnitude sanity check fires. I have deliberately excluded anything that is a special case of the listed E&M riders, the affine/log/hidden-quantity refuse classes, the CODATA-vintage tag, or the standard-state entry.

gaps.name: Uncertainty-statement semantics (probable error, split random/systematic, coverage factor, PDG scale factor)
gaps.what_breaks: The tool carries numeric values through a converter graph; any value with a ± carries an uncertainty that is dimensionally identical to the value, so no dimensional check can see that the ± means different statistical objects in different eras and communities. Pre-~1960 literature (and essentially all of Birge-era constants work) quotes a *probable error*; NBS/NPL-style calibration and pre-GUM metrology reports quote a random component as a multiple of the standard deviation plus separately-stated systematic bounds, to be combined by an unstated rule; post-1993 GUM practice quotes a combined standard uncertainty with an explicit coverage factor k (k=2 by convention at NIST); the PDG quotes 1σ but inflates discrepant averages by a scale factor S=[χ²/(N−1)]^{1/2}, and CODATA-style adjustments apply Birge-ratio expansion. Converting a value between unit systems while silently transporting the ± as if it were one standard deviation produces a stated precision that is wrong by up to 3×, and any downstream consistency check ('do these two papers agree?') is then wrong in the direction that manufactures false agreement or false tension.
gaps.magnitude: σ = PE/0.67449 = 1.4826 × PE (a 48% underestimate if a probable error is read as 1σ); ÷2 if a k=2 expanded uncertainty is read as 1σ; ÷3 for a '3 times the standard deviation' limit-of-error statement; up to √2 (or 2, for linear addition) from the choice of rule for combining separately-stated random and systematic components; PDG scale factors S routinely 1.2–2 and occasionally ~3.
gaps.example: Old style: 'X = 1.23456 ± 0.00021 (probable error)'. Modern rendering of the same measurement: X = 1.23456(31) with k=1, or X = 1.23456(62) with k=2. A tool that reads all three ± values as the same object concludes that three restatements of one measurement disagree by 3×. Same failure in reverse for 'X = 1.2345 ± 0.0004 (random, 3σ) ± 0.0011 (systematic limits)'.
gaps.fingerprint: Literal strings 'probable error', 'p.e.', 'limit of error', 'the quoted errors are three times the standard deviation', 'external/internal consistency', 'Birge ratio'; two ± groups on one value with (stat)/(syst) or (random)/(systematic) labels; 'expanded uncertainty', 'coverage factor k =', 'level of confidence 95 %'; PDG tables carrying an 'S =' annotation; publication era (probable error dominant before ~1955, essentially extinct after ~1970; GUM language only after 1993).

gaps.name: Air vs vacuum wavelength (the medium tag missing from the λ↔σ↔E converter edge)
gaps.what_breaks: The converter's reciprocal edge E = hc/λ, and any λ→wavenumber conversion, assumes λ is a vacuum wavelength. Standard spectroscopic practice — universal in pre-1970 line lists, still the default in solar/stellar spectroscopy and in NIST ASD's 'Obs. wavelength (air)' column — tabulates wavelengths above 2000 Å in *standard air* while tabulating wavenumbers and energy levels in vacuum. Both are lengths; the tool cannot see the difference. Worse, the correction is dispersive, so it is not even a constant scale factor that a downstream fit could absorb: it changes across a single line list. This is the single most common silent error I see in reused old atomic/molecular data.
gaps.magnitude: n(standard air) ≈ 1.000277 at 500 nm ⇒ 2.77×10⁻⁴ relative, i.e. 1.38 Å at 5000 Å, or 5.5 cm⁻¹ (166 GHz) — three to five orders of magnitude larger than the precision such line lists are quoted to (0.001–0.01 cm⁻¹). Dispersion: n runs from ≈1.000298 at 2000 Å to ≈1.000271 at 10000 Å, so the fractional error varies by ~10% across the optical range. (Related, much smaller: the 1927 international Ångström, defined via the Cd red line at 6438.4696 Å in standard air, differs from the SI Å by ~2×10⁻⁷.)
gaps.example: Line list entry 'λ = 5000.00 Å'. If air (the convention above 2000 Å): λ_vac = 5001.386 Å and σ = 19994.46 cm⁻¹. Naive vacuum reading: σ = 1/λ = 20000.00 cm⁻¹. Same dimensions, 5.54 cm⁻¹ apart.
gaps.fingerprint: Wavelength-valued symbols in Å or nm with values above 2000 Å in a spectroscopic table; explicit 'wavelengths in air', 'standard air (15 °C, 101 325 Pa, dry)', citations to Edlén 1953/1966, Birch & Downs, or Ciddor; a table carrying both λ and σ columns whose product is 1.000277×10⁸ rather than 10⁸ Å·cm⁻¹ (this is a self-fingerprinting check the tool can run); the 2000 Å convention boundary itself (a list that switches to vacuum below 2000 Å is an air list above it).

gaps.name: Pre-1961 atomic-mass scale: physical (¹⁶O = 16) vs chemical (natural O = 16) vs unified (¹²C = 12)
gaps.what_breaks: 'amu' before 1961 names two different units, neither of which is the unified u, and both coexisted in the same decade (physicists' physical scale, chemists' chemical scale). This is a unit *redefinition*, not a constants-vintage drift, so a CODATA-year tag does not catch it: the numeral 16.0000 means three different masses. Every mass defect, binding energy, Q-value, molar mass and Avogadro number in pre-1962 nuclear and physical-chemistry literature sits on one of these scales, and the tool's N-axis / molar-conventions machinery will happily map amu → u as identity.
gaps.magnitude: 1 amu(physical, ¹⁶O = 16) = 0.99968216 u (−3.178×10⁻⁴); 1 amu(chemical) = 0.999957 u (−4.3×10⁻⁵); physical/chemical ratio = 1.000275. Correspondingly N_A appears in period tables as 6.02486×10²³ (physical) vs 6.02252×10²³ (chemical), and the energy equivalent as ≈931.20 MeV per physical amu vs 931.494 MeV per u. 3×10⁻⁴ is 10–100× the precision such tables were quoted to.
gaps.example: A mass tabulated as '16.0000 amu' is 15.99491 u if the table is on the physical scale and 15.99931 u if it is on the chemical scale — a 0.0044 u (≈4 MeV) difference in a nuclear mass table. Equivalently, ¹²C is exactly 12 u but 12.00382 amu on the physical scale.
gaps.fingerprint: The token 'amu' rather than 'u' or 'Da'; publication before ~1962 (the transition ran 1959–1961, IUPAP/IUPAC); an explicit scale statement ('O¹⁶ = 16', 'chemical scale', 'physical scale'); N_A quoted as 6.0249×10²³ or 6.0225×10²³; ¹²C listed as 12.0038; the phrase 'atomic weight' with a table of non-integer O; a stated conversion 'M(phys) = 1.000275 M(chem)'.

gaps.name: kX / X-unit (Siegbahn) X-ray length scale and the vintage of its Å conversion factor
gaps.what_breaks: All X-ray wavelengths and crystallographic lattice parameters published before ~1948 (and many into the mid-1950s) are on the Siegbahn scale, defined by the calcite (200) spacing, in X units and kX. kX was *intended* to be the Ångström and was printed as if it were; it is not. A tool reading 'a = 3.6075 kX' as 3.6075 Å inherits a 0.21% length error that cubes into 0.62% on cell volumes and propagates straight into any derived density, Avogadro number, structure factor or Debye–Waller fit. Second-order trap: the conversion factor itself has a vintage, so 'converted to Å' in a 1949 paper is not the same Å as in a 1968 paper.
gaps.magnitude: 1 kX = 1.00207699(28) Å (CODATA, via xu(Cu Kα1)) ⇒ +2.077×10⁻³ on every length, +6.2×10⁻³ on volumes. The accepted factor drifted: 1.00202 (Bragg 1947) → 1.002056 → 1.0020772, a further 4×10⁻⁵ that exceeds the quoted precision of good 1950s cell-parameter work. Bearden's Å* scale (W Kα1 ≡ 0.2090100 Å*) is a third, distinct, near-Ångström length unit at the 10⁻⁵–10⁻⁶ level.
gaps.example: Cu Kα1 is 1.537400 kX ≡ 1.5405929 Å (1.537400 × 1.00207699). A paper quoting λ(Cu Kα1) = 1.5374 and a tool reading that as Ångström makes every d-spacing derived from it 0.21% too small. Similarly 'xu(Mo Kα1)' and 'xu(Cu Kα1)' are two different x units, differing by 2.3×10⁻⁵.
gaps.fingerprint: Unit tokens 'kX', 'X', 'X.U.', 'xu', 'kX.U.'; the words Siegbahn, calcite, '3029.04' or '3029.45'; publication before ~1950; λ(Cu Kα1) printed as 1.5374 or 1.539 rather than 1.5406; a 'Λ =' or 'conversion factor' line near 1.00202/1.002056/1.002077; the superscripted Å* symbol; lattice constants sitting a consistent ~0.2% below their modern values.

gaps.name: Era- and domain-gated homograph unit symbols (mK, K, μ, mμ, μμF, γ, λ, b)
gaps.what_breaks: The tool's lexicon presumably maps symbols to units by a modern table. Pre-1980 literature uses symbols that a modern table either mis-resolves or rejects, and the worst cases are the ones where both readings are dimensionally plausible energies/lengths of similar magnitude, so nothing downstream fires. The killer is mK: in atomic spectroscopy mK is the millikayser, 10⁻³ cm⁻¹ (NIST's own atomic-spectroscopy compendium uses it), while in the same hyperfine and low-temperature literature mK is the millikelvin — and via k_B/hc = 0.695035 cm⁻¹/K the two readings differ by only a factor 1.4388, which is exactly the regime no sanity check catches.
gaps.magnitude: 1.4388 for millikayser vs millikelvin (and for K = kayser vs kelvin); 10⁶ for μ read as the micro prefix instead of the micron (10⁻⁶ m); legacy double prefixes mμ (= nm) and μμF (= pF) are either rejected by a modern parser or mangled; γ is triply ambiguous — 10⁻⁵ Oe = 1 nT in geomagnetism, the microgram in older bio/Soviet literature, and a photon label — a quantity-kind swap, not a scale error; λ = microlitre in old chemistry; b = barn vs bar (10⁻²⁸ m² vs 10⁵ Pa).
gaps.example: 'A = 5 mK' in a hyperfine-structure paper: 5 millikayser = 5×10⁻³ cm⁻¹ = 149.9 MHz; 5 millikelvin = 104.2 MHz. Both are legitimate hyperfine constants, both are stated in mK by real papers, and the ratio is 1.4388.
gaps.fingerprint: Symbol resolution must be gated on (publication year, subfield, sibling quantities in the same table), not on a global table: 'mK' beside a term value in cm⁻¹ or an isotope shift → kayser; beside a dilution-refrigerator temperature → kelvin. Double-prefix tokens (mμ, μμ, mμF) are a hard era marker. A bare 'μ' followed by 'thick'/'diameter' is the micron. The correct behavior when context is absent is refusal, not a guess.

gaps.name: Gaussian magnetism reporting: 4πM quoted as the magnetization, G/Oe interchange, and bare 'emu'
gaps.what_breaks: cgs magnetism papers do not tabulate or plot M; they tabulate and plot 4πM in gauss, and they use gauss and oersted interchangeably for the applied field because B and H coincide numerically in vacuum. This is not the rationalization 4π the tool riders on D and H — the paper is internally consistent Gaussian throughout; 4πM is a *reporting label* for the ordinate. A translator that maps a y-axis labelled '4πM (kG)' onto SI M or μ₀M is off by 4π, and one that maps 'applied field 10 kG' onto B rather than μ₀H gets the right number in vacuum and the wrong quantity inside the sample. Separately, 'emu' is a moment (erg/G), so a susceptibility or magnetization 'in emu' with no volume, mass or mole basis has no dimensional preimage at all.
gaps.magnitude: 4π = 12.566 for the 4πM-vs-M label; inside matter B and H differ by exactly 4πM, which for iron is 21.5 kG — i.e. the error is the whole quantity, not a correction.
gaps.example: Iron, three self-consistent renderings of one fact: '4πM_s = 21.5 kG' (Gaussian, standard plotting convention) / 'M_s = 1714 emu cm⁻³' (Gaussian, magnetization proper) / 'M_s = 1.71×10⁶ A m⁻¹, μ₀M_s = 2.15 T' (SI). A tool that reads the first as M and the second as M gets two answers 4π apart.
gaps.fingerprint: Axis labels and table headings literally reading '4πM', '4πM_s (kG)', '4πM_eff'; the identity B = H + 4πM in the text; hysteresis loops with the ordinate in kG or G in a paper about a material; 'applied field' quoted in kG in a magnetization measurement (means H in kOe); demagnetizing factors N summing to 4π rather than 1; 'emu' with no denominator, or 'emu/g' vs 'emu/cm³' vs 'emu/mol' used interchangeably in one paper.

gaps.name: Spin-Hamiltonian parameters quoted in field units (A, D, E, linewidths in G/mT) — conversion needs the paper's fitted g
gaps.what_breaks: EPR, ENDOR, Mössbauer and older NMR papers quote hyperfine couplings, zero-field splittings and linewidths in gauss, oersted or millitesla, because that is what the magnet sweep reads. Converting them to frequency or energy is not a fixed spectroscopic equivalence: A[MHz] = (gμ_B/h)·A[G], so the conversion factor is a *fitted parameter of that paper*, not a constant. A converter with a spectroscopic-equivalence graph will apply the free-electron 2.8025 MHz/G (γ_e/2π = 28.024 GHz/T) universally. For organic radicals that is harmless; for transition-metal and rare-earth centres, where effective g values run from well below 1 to nearly 20, it is a large silent error, and dimensionally invisible because both readings are energies.
gaps.magnitude: Error factor = g_eff/2.0023. Benign (<0.2%) for free radicals; ×3.0 for a high-spin Fe(III) heme line at g_eff = 6; factors from ~0.25 to ~9 across rare-earth and high-spin effective g values; ×1.1 routinely for Cu(II) g∥ ≈ 2.2, which is already 10× the quoted precision of a hyperfine constant.
gaps.example: 'a = 100 G' converts to 280.2 MHz at g = 2.0023 but to 839.6 MHz at g_eff = 6.00 — same symbol, same unit, same dimension, factor 3.
gaps.fingerprint: A symbol named A, a, a_iso, D, E, ΔH_pp or ΔB_pp carrying G, Oe, or mT; a fitted g (or g∥/g⊥, g_x/g_y/g_z, g_eff) tabulated in the same table or caption; EPR/ENDOR/optical-detected-magnetic-resonance context; the tell-tale mixed table where some couplings are in MHz and others in gauss. Nuclear analogue: A in gauss with γ_N rather than γ_e.

gaps.name: Temperature-scale realization vintage (IPTS-27/48/68, EPT-76, ITS-90) as distinct from the affine °C↔K conversion
gaps.what_breaks: The tool treats temperature as an affine refuse class, which handles °C vs °F vs K but assumes a temperature *value* is scale-free once the offset is removed. It is not: t₆₈ and t₉₀ are different quantities realized by different interpolating instruments and fixed-point assignments, and every pre-1990 thermodynamic, calorimetric, vapour-pressure and radiometric datum carries its scale as part of its identity. Ratios of temperatures, Arrhenius and Planck-law fits over wide ranges, and comparisons of old and new fixed-point data all pick up a scale-dependent distortion that is not a constant offset and not a constant factor.
gaps.magnitude: T₉₀(Au) = T₆₈(Au) − 0.25 K at 1337 K (1.9×10⁻⁴ relative, and it enters the Planck extrapolation above the silver point amplified); the silver point moved from 961.93 °C (IPTS-68) to 961.78 °C (ITS-90); the t₉₀ − t₆₈ table is nonzero over the whole defined range, reaching a few tenths of a kelvin, and the IPTS-48 → IPTS-68 revision is larger still at high temperature. Below 5 K the ¹He/³He vapour-pressure scales (T₅₈, T₆₂) and EPT-76 differ from ITS-90 at the millikelvin level, which is the entire quantity for sub-kelvin work.
gaps.example: A radiance-temperature calibration reported as 'gold point = 1064.43 °C' is on IPTS-68; the same physical state is 1064.18 °C on ITS-90. A tool converting both to 1337.58 K and 1337.33 K respectively and then differencing them reports a 0.25 K physical discrepancy that does not exist.
gaps.fingerprint: Parenthetical scale tags '(IPTS-68)', '(IPTS-48)', '(ITS-27)', '(EPT-76)', '(ITS-90)', '°C (int.)'; publication-year windows (1948–1968, 1968–1990, post-1990); a stated gold-point value of 1063 (IPTS-48), 1064.43 (IPTS-68) or 1064.18 °C (ITS-90); citations to Preston-Thomas 1990 or to the 1968 amended edition; 'T₆₈', 'T₉₀', 't₆₈' as literal symbols.

gaps.name: Legacy unit names with several exact definitions (calorie, Btu, technical vs standard atmosphere, pre-1964 litre)
gaps.what_breaks: Several unit *names* that a modern table resolves to a single value are, historically, families of exactly-defined units that differ at the 10⁻⁴–10⁻² level — small enough to survive every dimensional check and every order-of-magnitude sanity check, large enough to swamp the precision the data were reported to. The choice is not era-only: it is discipline-correlated (steam tables and engineering → IT calorie/Btu; chemistry after 1948 → thermochemical), so the tool needs a domain-gated disambiguation and must refuse a bare symbol rather than pick a default. The 'at' case is a 3% error hiding in a one-letter difference from 'atm', endemic in German and Soviet high-pressure and thermodynamics literature.
gaps.magnitude: calorie: 4.184 J (thermochemical, exact) / 4.1868 J (IT, exact) / 4.1855 J (15 °C) / ≈4.190 J (mean) — spread 0.14%. Btu: 1054.35 J (thermochemical) to 1059.67 J (39 °F) — spread 0.50%. Technical atmosphere at = 1 kgf/cm² = 98066.5 Pa vs standard atmosphere atm = 101325 Pa — 3.32%. Pre-1964 litre = 1.000028 dm³ — 28 ppm on every density in g/ml from 1901–1964. 'ton': 907.18 / 1000 / 1016.05 kg, and the ton of TNT = 4.184 GJ by the thermochemical calorie.
gaps.example: 'ΔH = −57.80 kcal mol⁻¹' is −241.84 kJ mol⁻¹ on the thermochemical calorie and −242.00 kJ mol⁻¹ on the IT calorie — a 0.16 kJ mol⁻¹ split on a value quoted to 0.01. Likewise '300 at' is 29.42 MPa but '300 atm' is 30.40 MPa.
gaps.fingerprint: Bare 'cal', 'kcal', 'Btu' with no subscript; discipline and era (JANAF/NBS thermochemical tables and post-1948 chemistry → cal_th; ASME/IT steam tables and engineering heat transfer → cal_IT/Btu_IT); the tokens 'at', 'ata', 'atü', 'kp/cm²', 'кгс/см²', 'kgf/cm²' next to a pressure; 'ml' rather than 'cm³' in pre-1964 density and volumetric work; any paper that prints its own conversion line ('1 cal = 4.1840 J') — that line is the disambiguator and should be lifted as a per-paper custom generator.

found.overall: The tool is extremely strong on convention-as-algebra and essentially blind to convention-as-value-provenance. Two structural observations behind the nine entries. (1) The numeric converter graph needs quantity *qualifiers* that travel with the value, not just a dimension: a wavelength needs a medium tag, a temperature needs a scale-realization tag, a mass in amu needs a scale tag, a length in kX needs a scale-plus-conversion-vintage tag, and a ± needs uncertainty semantics. These are all the same schema move — a small set of orthogonal provenance slots on every numeric literal — and it is one design decision, not nine. The CODATA-vintage tag already in the plan is the first instance of this pattern; it should be generalized rather than special-cased, because unit *redefinitions* (amu 1961, litre 1964, Å/kX 1947, IPTS→ITS 1990) are a different animal from constant-value drift and a CODATA year does not encode them. (2) The unit lexicon must be era- and domain-gated, with refusal as the default on ambiguity. A global symbol table is actively harmful on pre-1980 material: mK, K, μ, γ, cal, at, b all resolve differently by year and subfield, and the failure mode is a factor of 1.44 or 1.03, never a factor of 10⁶, so nothing downstream catches it. I would ship items 1, 2 and 5 in v1 — they bite on any paper the tool reads out of the pre-1980 archive, including theory papers reusing old spectroscopic and constants data — and hold 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9 for v2 as domain packs (nuclear/chemical, crystallography, magnetism, magnetic resonance, thermometry, legacy engineering units).

verdict.lens: Metrology/experimental-history lens — convention carried by the *value* rather than the equation: unit realizations, epoch-dependent definitions, instrument-native units, medium/reference-state tags, and uncertainty semantics, all dimensionally invisible.

verdicts.gap: Uncertainty-statement semantics (probable error, split random/systematic, coverage factor, PDG scale factor)
verdicts.notes: All the numbers check out: PE = 0.67449σ so σ = 1.4826·PE; k=2 expanded → ÷2; '3× the s.d.' limits → ÷3; PDG S = [χ²/(N−1)]^{1/2} with S typically 1.2–2 and CODATA Birge-ratio expansion. Nothing in coverage or the round-3 exclusions touches uncertainty semantics (exclusion 5 is CODATA-vintage of the *value*, a different slot), so the gap is real and unlisted. But the stated failure mode is wrong: a unit conversion is a multiplication, so transporting ± through it preserves the *relative* uncertainty exactly, whatever statistical object the ± denotes — translation per se never 'produces a stated precision wrong by up to 3×'. The corrected claim: the ± semantics is a pure provenance tag with zero effect on the conversion arithmetic; it bites only on (a) re-rendering a value in modern (k=1/k=2) form, (b) any agree/disagree comparison across papers, (c) combining separately-stated random+systematic components. That narrows it to a tag plus a refuse-to-compare-across-semantics rule. v1 is defensible only if the tool ever compares or re-renders uncertainties; if it only transports them, this is v2.

verdicts.gap: Air vs vacuum wavelength (medium tag on the λ↔σ↔E converter edge)
verdicts.notes: Recomputed with Edlén (1966): (n−1)·10⁸ = 8342.13 + 2406030/(130−σ²) + 15997/(38.9−σ²), σ in μm⁻¹. At 500 nm → n−1 = 2.790e−4 (claim 2.77e−4, fine); 5000 Å ⇒ Δλ = 1.39 Å, Δσ = 5.54 cm⁻¹ = 166 GHz — example arithmetic (λ_vac 5001.39 Å, σ 19994.46 vs 20000.00 cm⁻¹) is exact. Dispersion: n−1 = 3.24e−4 at 2000 Å → 2.74e−4 at 10000 Å, i.e. the fractional correction varies ~18% across the optical range, not ~10% (understated, in the claim's favour). One overstatement: 5.54 cm⁻¹ against a 0.001–0.01 cm⁻¹ quoted precision is 2.7–3.7 orders of magnitude, not 'three to five'. The 2000 Å air/vacuum boundary and NIST ASD's dual air/vacuum columns are correct, as is the international Ångström (Cd 6438.4696 Å in standard air) at ~2e−7. The E = hc/λ reciprocal edge is explicitly in coverage but with no medium qualifier, and no exclusion covers this. The self-check (λ·σ = 1.000277e8 rather than 1e8 Å·cm⁻¹ on a dual-column table) is a genuinely good, cheap detector. v1 justified.

verdicts.gap: Pre-1961 atomic-mass scale: physical (¹⁶O=16) vs chemical (natural O=16) vs unified (¹²C=12)
verdicts.notes: Verified against the standard conversions 1 u = 1.0003179 amu(phys) = 1.000043 amu(chem), i.e. 1 amu(phys) = 0.9996822 u (−3.178e−4), 1 amu(chem) = 0.999957 u (−4.3e−5), chem/phys = 1.000275 — all as claimed. ¹⁶O = 15.9949146 u ⇒ 16 amu(phys) ≡ 15.99491 u exactly by definition; 16 amu(chem) = 15.99931 u; the 0.0045 u ≈ 4.2 MeV gap is right, as is ¹²C = 12.00382 amu(phys) and 931.20 vs 931.494 MeV. ONE FACTUAL ERROR in the fingerprint/magnitude: the paired Avogadro values are wrong. The historical pair is N_A(physical) = 6.02486e23 and N_A(chemical) = 6.02322e23 (ratio 1.000272 ≈ 1.000275). 6.02252e23 is the early-1960s value on the *unified* ¹²C scale, not the chemical-scale value — so 'N_A quoted as 6.0225e23' is a fingerprint for a post-1961 unified-scale paper, the opposite of what the entry says. Fix the fingerprint to 6.0249/6.0232. Gap itself is real, is a unit *redefinition* not a constant-value drift (correctly distinguished from exclusion 5), and is untouched by the N-axis/molar-conventions rows. v2 tier is right.

verdicts.gap: kX / X-unit (Siegbahn) X-ray length scale and the vintage of its Å conversion
verdicts.notes: Physics and magnitude correct. CODATA gives xu(CuKα1) = 1.00207697(28)e−13 m (claim writes 1.00207699 — last-digit slip, immaterial) and xu(MoKα1) = 1.00209952e−13 m, so the two x units differ by 2.25e−5 ✓ (claim 2.3e−5). 1 kX = 1000 xu(CuKα1) ⇒ +2.077e−3 on lengths, +6.24e−3 on volumes ✓. λ(CuKα1) = 1.537400 kX × 1.002077 = 1.540593 Å ✓. Bearden's Å* (W Kα1 ≡ 0.2090100 Å*) is a genuinely distinct near-Å unit, offset ~1.5e−5 from the SI Å ✓. Minor arithmetic slip: the drift 1.00202 → 1.002056 → 1.0020772 is 3.6e−5 then 2.1e−5 (5.7e−5 total), not 'a further 4e−5'. Calcite d(200) = 3029.04 XU (Siegbahn, 18 °C) ✓. Nothing in coverage or exclusions carries a length-scale-realization tag. v2 tier right (crystallography pack).

verdicts.gap: Era- and domain-gated homograph unit symbols (mK, K, μ, mμ, μμF, γ, λ, b)
verdicts.notes: The keystone case verified: millikayser = 10⁻³ cm⁻¹ is real and current in NIST-affiliated hyperfine work (e.g. FTS hyperfine-constant tables for Sc I/Sc II). k_B/hc = 0.6950348 cm⁻¹/K ⇒ 1 cm⁻¹ ≡ 1.438777 K, so 5 mK reads as 149.90 MHz (kayser) or 104.18 MHz (kelvin) — ratio 1.4388 exactly as claimed, and both are physically plausible hyperfine constants. The rest check out: γ = 10⁻⁵ Oe = 1 nT in geomagnetism and also the microgram in older bio/Soviet usage (a quantity-kind swap, correctly flagged); mμ = nm, μμF = pF; λ = μL; b = barn vs bar. Small looseness: a bare 'μ' read as a prefix is a *parse failure*, not a 10⁶ scale error — the 10⁶ only appears when micron is silently mapped to metre. Nothing in coverage (a systems table, not a lexicon spec) or the exclusions addresses symbol resolution; 'refuse when the disambiguating context is absent' is the right default given the tool's existing residual-rank-honesty posture. v1 justified. Note this and gap 9 are the same schema move and should ship as one era/domain-gated lexicon feature, not two.

verdicts.gap: Gaussian magnetism reporting: 4πM quoted as the magnetization, G/Oe interchange, bare 'emu'
verdicts.notes: Numbers correct: Fe M_s = 1714 emu/cm³ ⇒ 4πM_s = 21.54 kG ⇒ SI 1.714e6 A/m, μ₀M_s = 2.154 T; 4πM_eff, B = H + 4πM, and demagnetizing factors summing to 4π are all standard Gaussian practice. But the slotting is wrong on both halves. (a) The 'emu with no volume/mass/mole basis, and emu/g vs emu/cm³ vs emu/mol used interchangeably' half is literally exclusion (5) — quantity-kind tags, whose named example is χ_v/χ_mol/χ_g. Duplicate. (b) The genuinely new half — '4πM' as an ordinate/symbol label inside a fully self-consistent Gaussian paper — is NOT a rider. Riders in this tool activate on system conversion when a factor lies outside the span of restored generators; here no system conversion is happening and the paper is internally consistent, so a rider table would fire on the wrong trigger and would also collide with the registry entry χ_SI = 4πχ_cgs, which is the same 4π seen through susceptibility. Correct home: a symbol-alias / quantity-kind declaration ('the tabulated ordinate is 4πM, not M'; 'applied field in kG means H in kOe'), i.e. an extension of the quantity-kind tag slot already in exclusion 5 — plus, optionally, a per-paper custom generator when the paper states B = H + 4πM. Confidence 'likely' is appropriately hedged; scope it down to the label-aliasing claim.

verdicts.gap: Spin-Hamiltonian parameters in field units (A, D, E, linewidths in G/mT) needing the paper's fitted g
verdicts.notes: Physics and magnitudes exact: gμ_B/h = 2.80245 MHz/G at g = 2.0023 (γ_e/2π = 28.0245 GHz/T); at g_eff = 6.00 the factor is 8.397 MHz/G, so 100 G → 839.7 MHz, ratio 3.00 ✓. g∥ ≈ 2.2 for Cu(II) gives 1.10 ✓; g_eff = 6 for high-spin Fe(III) heme ✓; rare-earth/Ising-doublet g up to ~18–20 supports the 0.25–9 span ✓. The mis-slot is 'refuse_class'. Every listed refuse class is non-invertible in principle (log, affine, Möbius, similarity variable, no dimensional preimage). This one is perfectly invertible the moment g is known, and the entry's own fingerprint concedes g is normally tabulated in the same table or caption. It therefore belongs in the machinery the tool already has: a per-paper CUSTOM generator (g lifted from the paper, with the existing rank check), with refusal only as the fallback when no g is stated. Also flag partial overlap with the existing 'NMR/EPR' and 'spectroscopic equivalences' rows — the new content is specifically that the equivalence is a fitted per-paper parameter, not that gauss↔MHz exists.

verdicts.gap: Temperature-scale realization vintage (IPTS-27/48/68, EPT-76, ITS-90) vs the affine °C↔K conversion
verdicts.notes: Correct and correctly distinguished from the affine refuse class: t₆₈ and t₉₀ are different realizations, and t₉₀ − t₆₈ is a non-constant, non-affine, non-multiplicative table. Values verified: Au point 1064.43 °C (IPTS-68) → 1064.18 °C (ITS-90), Δ = 0.25 K = 1.87e−4 relative; Ag point 961.93 → 961.78 °C; IPTS-48 Au point 1063 °C; t₉₀ − t₆₈ nonzero throughout, a few tenths of a K at the top; EPT-76 and the T₅₈ (⁴He) / T₆₂ (³He) vapour-pressure scales differ from ITS-90 at the mK level, which is indeed the whole quantity below 1 K. The example (1337.58 vs 1337.33 K, a spurious 0.25 K 'discrepancy') is arithmetically right. One naming slip: the 1927 scale is ITS-27, not IPTS-27 (the 'IPTS' prefix dates from the 1960 amendment of the 1948 scale) — the fingerprint list gets this right, the title does not. Not covered anywhere; not the CODATA-vintage tag. v2 tier right.

verdicts.gap: Legacy unit names with several exact definitions (calorie, Btu, technical vs standard atmosphere, pre-1964 litre)
verdicts.notes: Every number checks: cal_th = 4.184 J exact, cal_IT = 4.1868 J exact, cal_15 = 4.1855 J, cal_mean ≈ 4.190 J (0.14% full spread, 0.067% for the th/IT pair that actually matters); Btu_th = 1054.35 J, Btu_IT = 1055.056 J, Btu_39°F = 1059.67 J (0.50% spread); at = 1 kgf/cm² = 98066.5 Pa vs atm = 101325 Pa = 3.32% (300 at = 29.42 MPa, 300 atm = 30.40 MPa ✓); litre 1901–1964 = 1.000028 dm³ = 28 ppm; ton 907.18/1000/1016.05 kg; ton TNT = 1e9 cal_th = 4.184 GJ. Example verified: −57.80 kcal/mol = −241.84 (th) vs −242.00 (IT) kJ/mol. Two scoping corrections. (i) The 'at / kgf/cm² / кгс/см²' case is partly reachable from the existing gravitational-metric (MKpS) system row — the *value* is already known; what is missing is only the at-vs-atm lexical disambiguation, so don't sell this as a new system. (ii) This is the same schema move as gap 5 (era/domain-gated lexicon, refusal on ambiguity) applied to a different token set, and should be merged with it rather than shipped as a separate converter_entry family. The 'lift the paper's own printed conversion line (1 cal = 4.1840 J) as a per-paper custom generator' proposal is good and reuses machinery the tool already has. Confidence 'likely' understates it — the unit values are exact and documented; v2 tier is right.

verdict.overall: Strong round: the lens is genuinely orthogonal to everything in coverage and the round-3 exclusions, which are all algebra-side. Seven of nine survive intact on physics and magnitude; recomputation found only cosmetic slips (a 1966-Edlén dispersion span understated at 10% vs the true ~18%, 'three to five orders' for what is 2.7–3.7, the kX drift quoted as 4e−5 vs 5.7e−5, ITS-27 mislabelled IPTS-27) plus one substantive factual error worth fixing before it ships: gap 3 pairs N_A(physical) = 6.02486e23 with 6.02252e23 as the 'chemical' value — the chemical-scale value is 6.02322e23, and 6.02252e23 is an early-1960s *unified* ¹²C value, so that fingerprint currently points the wrong way. Three entries need re-slotting rather than rejection. Gap 1's stated failure mode is wrong (unit conversion is a multiplication and preserves relative uncertainty under any ± semantics; the gap is a provenance tag that bites on re-rendering and cross-paper comparison, not on translation) — keep it, but as tag-plus-refuse-to-compare, and its v1 claim depends on whether the tool ever compares. Gap 6 splits: its emu-basis half is exclusion (5) quantity-kind tags verbatim, and its surviving 4πM-ordinate half is a symbol-alias, not a rider — routing it to the rider table would fire on the wrong trigger and collide with the registry's χ_SI = 4πχ_cgs. Gap 7 is invertible given the paper's fitted g and so is not a refuse class; it belongs in the existing per-paper custom-generator machinery with refusal only as fallback. Finally, gaps 5 and 9 are one feature (era/domain-gated lexicon with refusal as default), not two, and the author's own closing paragraph — one set of orthogonal provenance slots on every numeric literal, generalizing the CODATA-vintage tag — is the right architectural read and worth adopting over the nine-entries framing. Net: gaps 2, 3, 4, 5, 8, 9 confirmed as new (subject to the corrections above), gap 1 confirmed-but-narrowed, gaps 6 and 7 partially duplicated and mis-slotted.
